patient.chief_complaint: Continuous generalized seizure for 20 minutes, known epilepsy, missed antiepileptic medications for 3 days
patient.history_present_illness: A 36-year-old White male software engineer with a 10-year history of juvenile myoclonic epilepsy (JME) was brought to the emergency department by his girlfriend via EMS after a continuous generalized tonic-clonic seizure at home. His girlfriend reports he began convulsing while watching television at approximately 9:45 PM. He initially had bilateral arm jerking (myoclonic) that rapidly evolved into a full generalized tonic-clonic seizure and continued without stopping. EMS was called 5 minutes after onset. He arrived continuously convulsing — total seizure duration at ED arrival was 22 minutes. EMS administered IV lorazepam 4 mg enroute without effect. He has a longstanding diagnosis of JME confirmed by video-EEG 8 years ago, showing 3-4 Hz generalized polyspike-wave discharges with prominent morning myoclonic jerks. He was well-controlled on valproate 1500 mg/day for 6 years until 2 years ago when he was switched to levetiracetam 1500 mg BID due to weight gain. He has been stable with levetiracetam. His girlfriend reports he ran out of levetiracetam 3 days ago and was trying to 'get by' until his next prescription was refilled. He works long hours and had been sleep-deprived for the past week (known JME trigger). No alcohol or drug use. No fever. No recent illness. He has no medication allergies. Family history: sister has absence epilepsy. Social history: non-smoker, occasional beer on weekends (none this week per girlfriend), no illicit drugs. He is a software engineer currently working remotely on a deadline project.

interactions: Phenytoin/fosphenytoin + JME (idiopathic generalised epilepsy): CONTRAINDICATED — phenytoin blocks fast sodium channels but does NOT suppress thalamocortical T-type calcium channel circuits mediating JME myoclonus; paradoxically worsens myoclonic and absence components; multiple case series demonstrate clinical deterioration.
contraindications: Phenytoin and fosphenytoin: absolutely contraindicated in JME and all idiopathic generalised epilepsies — worsens myoclonus and absence seizures.
warnings: NEVER use phenytoin or fosphenytoin in JME. For JME SE: IV lorazepam + IV levetiracetam loading. If refractory: IV valproate is second-line (effective for JME but teratogenic in women of childbearing age). Lamotrigine is third-line for chronic JME management.
alternatives: IV levetiracetam 2000 mg loading dose — first-line for JME SE
IV valproate 20-30 mg/kg — second-line if levetiracetam insufficient

results.title: Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy: long-term outcomes and management
results.key_finding: JME is a lifelong epilepsy requiring maintenance AED therapy. Key triggers for breakthrough seizures and SE: sleep deprivation, alcohol, medication non-adherence (strongest predictor). Levetiracetam and valproate are most effective for JME. Phenytoin/carbamazepine/vigabatrin worsen JME. Medication adherence education and automated refill programs reduce breakthrough SE risk by 70%. Most JME patients require lifelong treatment.

output.summary: Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy (JME) is a lifelong condition requiring maintenance antiepileptic therapy. Key seizure triggers include sleep deprivation, alcohol, and medication non-adherence — the last being the strongest predictor of breakthrough events including status epilepticus. Levetiracetam and valproate are the most effective antiepileptic drugs for JME. Phenytoin, carbamazepine, and vigabatrin may paradoxically worsen JME. Medication access strategies such as automated prescription refill programmes are associated with reduced breakthrough seizure risk. Most patients with JME require lifelong treatment.

IV levetiracetam 2000 mg loading dose — restore therapeutic level
Phenytoin/fosphenytoin ABSOLUTELY CONTRAINDICATED in JME — worsens myoclonus and absence

contraindicated_actions: Phenytoin or fosphenytoin for JME SE — contraindicated in idiopathic generalized epilepsy, worsens myoclonus and absence seizures
Carbamazepine for long-term JME management — worsens absence and myoclonic components
Discharging without levetiracetam refill — prescription lapse was the direct cause; must provide refill before discharge
key_reasoning_points: JME + undetectable AED level = medication non-adherence is the precipitant — the most common cause of SE in patients with known epilepsy

Phenytoin/fosphenytoin CONTRAINDICATED in JME — blocks fast Na+ channels in cortical neurons but does not suppress the thalamocortical T-type calcium channel circuits mediating JME; can paradoxically worsen myoclonus
Levetiracetam IV loading is the correct approach: 2000 mg IV bolus restores therapeutic levels rapidly, safe and effective
JME triggers are critical counseling points: sleep deprivation, alcohol, medication non-adherence — all three were present in this case
Post-ictal leukocytosis is a stress response, not infection — do not initiate empiric antibiotics based on WBC elevation alone in a post-ictal patient with clear precipitant
Serial troponin trending down confirms neurogenic cardiac stress, not NSTEMI — differentiation from Type 2 MI requires trending
